title: Beam Model Technical Report
text: Beam is a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 501.3B total parameters and 23.4B active parameters, specifically built and optimized for coding, reasoning, and agentic workloads. Beam delivers frontier level reasoning, while requiring 3-4x less inference compute than many models of its class. Pretrained on 23.8T diverse, curated, high-quality tokens, Beam features a 1M-token context window achieved through a novel two-stage midtraining phase, built on verifiable, correctness-anchored data. Post-training leveraged a large-scale, fully asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) campaign across 10.5K GB300 GPUs, generating over 100M rollouts over 4 weeks of training. We believe this is one of the largest scale RL runs conducted by any open lab to date. Across our evaluation suite, capabilities continued to improve as we increased RL compute, with no sign of a plateau. Supported by deep hardware-model co-design, FP8/NVFP4 quantization, and a 1.93B-parameter speculative decoding drafter (DFlash 2), Beam maximizes serving throughput with efficient, flexible deployment. Averaged across conversation turns and harm categories, Beam refuses or pivots on 88.9% of harmful requests while complying with 81.5% of harmless requests, achieving the highest refusal/pivot rate on harmful requests among open-weight models on the Pareto frontier.

title: DexDuet: Learning Contact-Preserving Bimanual Dexterity from Human Demonstrations
text: Human demonstrations provide a rich source of bimanual dexterous skills, yet transferring them to robot hands remains challenging. Existing methods primarily optimize object trajectory tracking, often overlooking how human hands interact with the object. Even with accurate tracking, robots may contact incorrect object parts or slide their fingers, resulting in unstable manipulation. We present DexDuet, a framework that learns contact-preserving bimanual dexterity from a single human demonstration. DexDuet employs two interaction rewards to preserve human hand-object configurations and contacts. To enable coordinated manipulation, we factorize the bimanual policy into two weight-sharing per-hand policies that condition on each other's states. We further propose assisted reference-state initialization (A-RSI), an adaptive curriculum that adjusts object assistance and training starts across demonstration segments to overcome difficult manipulation phases. Across four benchmarks spanning three simulators and five robot embodiments, DexDuet improves object-tracking ADD-AUC by 11 to 41 points over the corresponding baselines while consistently achieving better contact preservation. Notably, among 122 paired runs with comparable object-tracking accuracy, DexDuet preserves the human's contacts better in 117 cases. Code and videos are available at https://rcl-robotics.github.io/Dexduet.io/

title: Single-Transformer Latent Diffusion
text: Latent generative models typically rely on three separate networks: an encoder that tokenizes pixels, a generator that models the latent distribution, and a decoder that maps latents back to pixels. UNITE recently merged the first two into a single generative encoder trained in one stage, but its decoder remains a separate network. We ask whether this last network can be folded in too, so that one diffusion transformer encodes, generates, and decodes. Simply letting the shared backbone decode does not help. What makes it work is to cast all three modes as position-aligned sequence maps over one fully shared backbone, distinguished only by a mode token and the timestep. The resulting model, UNIFIED, is simple: one network trained from scratch in a single stage with only reconstruction and flow-matching losses, without adversarial losses or pretrained encoders (e.g., DINO). On ImageNet-1K 256x256 at matched parameters, UNIFIED improves gFID over UNITE at three sizes (~60M, ~115M, and ~215M) and reaches 2.08 with 215M parameters, the lowest among compared models under 250M parameters. On text-to-image generation, UNIFIED-B (218M) reaches a GenEval score of 0.87 at 512x512, exceeding single-stage pixel diffusion models with around one billion parameters. Full unification of latent diffusion is thus not merely feasible but beneficial.

title: Can Latent Reasoning Drive LLM Outputs Without a Trace?
text: LLMs typically solve complex tasks with chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, which is also the main tool for monitoring them for misaligned behavior. However, standard transformers can also solve tasks with complete latent reasoning (CLR), carrying out the whole task internally and outputting only the final answer. Theory bounds the depth of CLR, the number of sequential steps it can carry out, and recent work measured it to be shallow. In this work, we ask whether CLR is deep enough for a model to pursue a hidden objective that requires reasoning. Such a model would generate a CoT that appears to solve the given task, while a latent multi-step computation decides its answer based on the hidden objective. First, we show that a simple auxiliary loss allows models to solve a multi-step task latently at least 5x deeper than previously reported. Then, in two common tasks, decision-making and code generation, we train a model to pursue such a hidden objective, which decides a loan or plants a vulnerability. The model's CoT justifies the output with no trace of the hidden objective, and a strong LLM monitor does not flag it. Finally, using activation patching, we find that the latent computation is completed before the model generates its CoT, which takes no part in it. Altogether, we show that a hidden objective that requires reasoning can go unseen by a monitor that reads only the output.

title: Unlocking the Power of Loops in Pretrained LLMs with Loop Residuals
text: Looped Transformers iterate a shared block of layers to increase computation without adding parameters, offering stronger performance and test-time scaling. However, this power has so far required training from scratch and yielded only modest gains for LLMs. Finetuning existing models into loops is far cheaper, yet also brings only marginal gains over SFT. We propose LoopRes, an effective, scalable, and simple approach that turns loops into significant and consistent gains for pretrained LLMs. Building on Attention Residuals, LoopRes lets each looped layer attend directly to the outputs of earlier loops. Since these outputs are iterates of the same layers and become harder to tell apart, we give each a trainable loop-aware key that encodes its structural identity. Attending to all earlier loops also lets layers skip intermediate ones, so we restrict each layer to a residual window of the latest W loops, forcing every loop to build incrementally on recent ones. Across 6 pretrained LLMs from 3 model families and 9 benchmarks, LoopRes delivers significant and consistent gains: at 2x compute, it improves Qwen3-1.7B-Base by 29.1% over SFT, more than doubling the gain of the state-of-the-art baseline. The gains hold on larger models up to 30B and across all three families. More importantly, from 1.7B to 8B, LoopRes scales more steeply than SFT as compute grows, reaching a higher ceiling while needing less compute on long outputs. These results establish LoopRes as an effective looping approach, delivering both better performance and better test-time scaling.

title: LLMs Memorize Their Own Hallucinations During Post-Training
text: Reasoning domains have shaped the post-training recipes of frontier models even though they are trained and deployed in domains beyond math and code. In this paper, we study the consequences of directly adopting reasoning-centric training recipes, e.g., the use of outcome-based rewards for reinforcement learning (RL), injection of "cognitive" behaviors such as proposing and backtracking from hypotheses in reasoning chains, etc., for knowledge tasks. We hypothesize that these decisions, while useful for reasoning, inadvertently encourage models to memorize hallucinations they themselves generate in their long reasoning chains when trained on knowledge tasks. To study this, we train models with standard post-training, extract their self-generated hallucinations during RL, and track memorization throughout the rest of training. Our experiments on six open models across two model families and two architectures confirm our hypothesis. We find that models' recall of hallucinations reinforced during training increases by 4.83% on average, compared to just 0.17% for self-hallucinations that receive no training signal. In fact, models even memorize false facts that they immediately retract in their reasoning; a backtracking template inherited from reasoning-centric training that has no benefit for knowledge recall. Furthermore, we find that memorization is strongest on the hardest training questions, and rewarding a hallucination makes the model less likely to abstain from it later (by 7.23% on average). Overall, our work identifies and systematically studies a previously unexamined pathway through which models learn hallucinations during training.

title: Measuring and Teaching Language Model Agents to Act on Delayed Consequences
text: Language model agents are increasingly asked to run ongoing multi-day operations rather than finish isolated single-turn tasks. In daily operations, today's choices reshape later observations and cash constraints because empty shelves hide lost walk-in demand, short-shipped customers quietly shrink future orders weeks later, and emergency buying drains working capital. We introduce SMB Bench, a calibrated 90-day wholesale simulator with 18 causally paired tasks and an 859-run frontier trace dataset, to ask what experience and learning signal make an agent better at noticing, attributing, and acting on the delayed consequences of its own decisions in unseen businesses. Across 16 frontier models, only 3 outperform a fixed buying rule; models often record a relevant diagnosis in their notes without changing later purchases in time, showing that diagnosing a problem, changing behavior, and improving a business are separate achievements. To study how experience improves those failures in an open model (Qwen3.8-27B), we used training-business records to identify operational rules and archived frontier quarters as starting states to continue from rather than transcripts to copy. On an unseen test business under identical evaluation instructions, the trained policy followed customer-protection commitments more consistently and reduced severe-loss quarters, while the additional profit benefit remained uncertain. Carrying those commitments through the quarter exposed the cost of fulfilling them, as early-quarter stocking habits left the buyer relying on emergency supply and a deteriorating supplier. The results separate recognizing a delayed effect, acting on it consistently, and coordinating surrounding decisions so that the response improves profit. SMB Bench connects these observations to a learning method by turning archived decisions and their consequences into reusable training experience.

title: Innata-0: A Native Embodied World System with Model-Agent Co-Design
text: The physical world is open-ended, dynamic, and partially observable. While foundation models have advanced embodied intelligence, standalone models struggle with long-horizon execution, and simply integrating models with agents may lead to inconsistencies between planning and physical control. To support reliable and adaptive behaviors in the physical world, we introduce Innata-0, a native embodied world system. Innata-0 jointly designs an embodied world-action model and an agent to combine their complementary strengths. The model, Innata-0-WAM, adopts a tri-tower Mixture-of-Transformers architecture that integrates understanding, prediction, and action generation. The agent, Innata-0-Agent, coordinates long-horizon execution through memory, verification, and recovery. A co-design protocol is further proposed to align model training with agent execution and leverage validated experiences to support subsequent adaptation and model improvement. Extensive evaluations demonstrate strong embodied capabilities across understanding, world prediction, and robotic manipulation. Innata-0 represents our first step toward physical intelligence, and we see it as the beginning of a much longer journey.

text: Anthropic Staff Openly Talk About ‘Taking Over the World’, Claims Top MIT Physicist Apparently they discuss overthrowing the US government after a few drinks. Employees at US artificial intelligence company Anthropic openly talk about “overthrowing the US government” and “taking over the world”, a world-renowned physicist has claimed. In an interview with Novara Media, Max Tegmark, a professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, said: “When I talk to people who work for Anthropic, after they’ve had a couple of drinks, the conversation often gets into overthrowing the US government and taking over the world.” “They tend to not use words like ‘coup’ and ‘overthrow the US government’. They instead use the code phrase ‘alignment without control’,” he said. ‘Alignment without control’ is the idea that AI should be kept in check by being instilled with certain values – likely those shared by Anthropic, Tegmark said – rather than being directly controlled by humans. “We get the sort of future that Alan Turing predicted, where it’s going to be Anthropic’s machine-god running Earth, and then the rest of us just have to hope that somehow it’s gonna be nice.” Turing, widely regarded as the founder of computer science, famously warned in 1951 that once machines started thinking, we should expect them to take control. Tegmark said the comments from Anthropic staff should alarm anyone who cares about democracy. “These companies really don’t seem to like it [democracy]. They have lobbied really hard to even prevent any meaningful government oversight of them,” he said. He added: “Here in the US, OpenAI and Anthropic are less regulated than a sandwich shop.” Novara Media has approached Anthropic for comment. title: LLM agents work for their parent companies, not for you
text: In the evenings after work, I will often sit out back on the porch and do some phone rotting. That usually takes the form of me just flipping through reels on Instagram, allowing the algorithm to take me where it may. I usually pair this with a healthy tumbler of rum or bourbon. I'm turning my brain off after work, and I'm just having a good time on the internet. The kids might call it dopamine maxxing? Hell, I don't know. Who gives a shit about what those assholes would call it? Anywho, I often encounter songs I really really like, and I would like to listen and discover more of please. Instagram makes it hard for me to connect with the band outside of their platform. I was trying to make this connection manually myself at first. I would just email myself a reel from my phone. Then when I'm back on the sofa and in the mood to track down new music, I'd open the reels and do my best to search on Bandcamp or YouTube or try to figure out if some of these musicians had a way to buy music from them. Very few do these days. They send you their Spotify link or send you to their TikTok page. I don't want to do any of that. I'd like to trade US dollars in exchange for some music files I can download onto my computer, where I can listen as much as I like on any device I own thank you please. Retro maxxing. So, I used Claude Code to build a skill that does this for me. It opens the Instagram reel and attempts to identify the artist and song. It then tries to determine if the artists have a Bandcamp page so I can purchase the songs I want, and if it finds one, it gives me the URL so I can click it to complete the trade I want. I want to buy music from artists who make music I like. That's a fair and wholesome endeavor, I feel, but this recently stopped working. It turns out Bandcamp added a challenge on their search API page. Ah bummer. No worries, that was an unpublished workaround anyway. As I was mulling over this discovery, the robot went on to explain that it would not help me work around the challenge. cue Nick Young question marks Well, that led me down a whole nother rabbit hole, which is turning into this post. There's another branch of my skill that attempts to locate the same song from the Instagram reel on YouTube, and it'll download the song to my computer if I ask. So let me get this straight. The robot, which is my robot that I pay a pretty penny for, will not attempt to work around the challenge at Bandcamp so that I can more easily connect with bands to complete a sale, but it will download the YouTube song, which doesn't send any money to the band or anyone??? This is the real danger of the frontier AI models. Not that it won't help me hack Bandcamp[1], but that this model doesn't really work for us. Well, they do, but only insofar as Anthropic or OpenAI or whoever else allows them to. In this case, Anthropic is trying to ensure that people can't use their models for evil. I'm not trying to do evil. I'm actually trying to do good! I want to buy something from a small artist on the internet. That's basically the most wholesome thing a person can do on the internet! Have no doubt, dear reader, these companies want to dominate. They want to capture the market. They want all the money. It'll be the same march to enshittification that happened with Google. A bunch of nerds who built something cool sold out, and it turned into just another business that decided to remove its don't be evil mantra. Right now, I think the robots are providing real information to the best of their ability, but I think it's only a matter of time until we must wonder if the answers they're providing are real answers that the robot found, or if they're weighted answers Anthropic put there because a company gave it enough money for product placement. I want to know the best robot vacuum according to old reddit or other trusted sources like Wirecutter, weighed and measured according to what I, and thus my robot agent, think are important requirements.

text: Less code, same tests passing: delete the dead code, files, dependencies and assets in any codebase, and keep each cut only if your own tests still pass.. Less code. Same tests passing. Coding agents write code faster than anyone deletes it. Functions nothing calls, files nothing imports, packages nothing uses, images nothing shows: your agent reads all of it, your CI builds it, your users download it. shrink-anything finds it, deletes it, and runs your own tests after every cut. What passes stays. What breaks is put back. One command, fully reversible. Every line it removes is a line your agent stops reading on the next task. The report counts that too: on the demo app, 46% fewer tokens to read. Install Use Or step by step: command | what it does | scan | lists what could go. Changes nothing | cut -- | deletes what's dead and runs your check: what passes stays, what breaks is put back | task --agent claude | hands the judgment calls (duplicates, public methods) to your agent, and keeps its work only if the check agrees | weigh dist | where the weight of a build is: by kind of file, the heaviest files, what's in there twice | verify | runs your check now, against the test count from before the first cut | undo | takes the last cut back, byte for byte (--all for every cut) | report | markdown + SVG card for your PR | doctor | what's installed: parsers, package managers, agents | --agent takes claude, codex, or any command that reads a prompt on stdin. Without it, hand .shrink/TASK.md to whatever you use. Proof, not vibes Nothing in that code mentions secretlyused: a test reaches it through a name it reads from a data file. The cut broke that test, so it was put back, alone. Your check decides. A cut stays only if your command exits 0 and at least as many tests run as before. A check that already fails is refused: it can't prove anything. One bad cut doesn't sink the rest. Cuts go in as a batch. If the check fails, the batch is split until the one cut that breaks it is found and put back. Every state left on disk has passed. Parsed before it's tested. Each edited file goes through the language's own parser (Python, Node, Ruby, PHP, Lua, Bash) before your check runs. Tests are never touched, and shrink-anything undo restores every file byte for byte. What can't be proven isn't cut. A public method, an export of a library, a subclass a framework may register, a file in a folder loaded by convention: these go to your agent with the reason, or behind --aggressive. The proof is as strong as your check. A project with no tests gets a scan, not a cut you should trust. What it finds | how it decides | where | dead code | every mention of the name is inside its own definition. Any other mention anywhere (another file, a string, a template, a config) keeps it | 19 languages | dead files | no other file names it | Python, JS/TS, PHP, Ruby, Dart, Lua/Luau | unused dependencies | nothing imports it or runs its commands | npm · pnpm · yarn · bun · Cargo · pip · Go modules | dead weight | an image, font or sound no code, config or README names; the same file stored twice | any project | duplicates | the same code twice, whatever it's called and however it's laid out | 19 languages, merged by your agent | It counts names instead of building a call graph. A count can only miss dead code, never invent it, and it works the same in every language. Results The demo projects in examples/, each with planted dead code. Run them yourself. project | before | after | TypeScript cart | 106 lines, 5 files, 3 dependencies | 58 lines, 3 files, 1 dependency (−45%) | Python shop | 142 lines, 8 files | 86 lines, 7 files (−39%) | Go store | 89 lines | 55 lines (−38%) | Static site (build output) | 913 KB | 398 KB (−56%) | On real projects expect less per run and more over time: the safe cuts go on their own, the rest is a reviewed list. Lighter builds --size takes a build folder or a binary and reports it before and after. Fewer dependencies and less code mean a smaller bundle; unused assets are cut like dead code. Assets in a folder served as it is (public/, static/) need --aggressive: a page outside your repo may link to them. Agents Claude Code plugin: /plugin marketplace add EL4CTEO/shrink-anything, then /plugin install shrink-anything@shrink-anything and /shrink-anything:shrink npm test MCP server (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor…), built into the binary: claude mcp add shrink-anything -- shrink-anything mcp. 8 tools: shrinkscan, shrinkcut, shrinktask, shrinkverify, shrinkundo, shrinkreport, shrinkweigh, shrinkstatus. Skill: skills/shrink-anything teaches any agent the loop. Languages Dead code and duplicates: Python · JavaScript · TypeScript · Rust · Go · Java · Kotlin · C# · C · C++ · PHP · Ruby · Swift · Dart · Lua · Luau · Elixir · Shell. Every other text file (HTML, Vue, Svelte, YAML, SQL, templates…) is read for mentions, so a function used only from a template stays. A language is one entry in a table (src/lang.rs): how its comments and strings look, how a block ends, what a definition looks like. Adding one is a pull request of about twenty lines. Library or app? In a library, public names belong to its users, so they're kept. shrink-anything guesses per language (a published package.json, a lib.rs, no package main) and says what it guessed. Override with --lib or --app. License MIT

title: w1ccc/sap-data-mcp: Read-only MCP servers that let AI assistants query SAP S/4HANA through RFC/BAPI, private-cloud OData and public-cloud re
text: Read-only MCP servers that let AI assistants query SAP S/4HANA through RFC/BAPI, private-cloud OData and public-cloud released APIs. Every call audited; credentials stay local.. SAP Data MCP 一句话，读懂你的 S/4HANA。 让 Claude 等 AI 助手只读查询 SAP S/4HANA 的 MCP 服务，RFC/BAPI、私有云 OData、公有云 API 都能接 English · 3 步上手 · 完整宣传片 · MIT 许可 一句话理解：如果把 AI 助手看成一位新同事，SAP Data MCP 就是给它开的一个只读账号，外加一本操作手册：订单、发票、库存、供应商未清项，它都能自己去 SAP 里查，再用一句话把结论告诉你；但它改不了任何数据，碰不到你的密码，查过什么也都有记录。 3 步上手 需要 Python 3.12，以及一个支持 MCP 的 AI 工具，例如 Claude Desktop、Claude Code 或 Cursor。下面以公有云 API 为例（Windows PowerShell）： 1. 打开 publiccloud\api\.env，填写系统地址 SAPAPIBASEURL，再选 Basic 认证（SAPAPIUSERNAME、SAPAPIPASSWORD）或 OAuth 客户端凭证（SAPAPIAUTH=oauth、SAPAPITOKENURL、SAPAPICLIENTID、SAPAPICLIENTSECRET）。私有云 OData 的做法一样，把目录换成 privatecloud\odata。 2. 把服务注册到 AI 工具，路径换成你的实际位置： Claude Code 里一行就行：claude mcp add sappublicapi -- C:\sap-data-mcp\.venv\Scripts\python.exe C:\sap-data-mcp\publiccloud\api\server.py 3. 让 AI 先调用 healthcheck 和 testsapapiconnection(service="material") 确认连通，然后直接用中文提问，比如「PO 4500000417 的货款怎么还没到？」 本地部署和私有云如果走 RFC/BAPI，还需要 SAP NW RFC SDK 和 PyRFC，按 GOLDENPATH.md 配置。每个服务都从自己 server.py 所在的目录读取 .env、config/ 和 logs/，所以 AI 工具里只要写绝对路径。 和其他做法有什么不同 你可能用过的做法 | 麻烦在哪里 | SAP Data MCP 的不同 | 在 SAP GUI 里手工查（ME23N、MIR4、FBL1N…） | 一个问题要开好几个事务码，单号来回复制，还会被「填写所有必填字段」拦下 | 用中文提问，AI 自己调用对应的标准读取接口，一次给出结论 | 自己写脚本调 RFC 或 OData | 每个新问题都要写代码、处理认证和分页，脚本里还常常带着密码 | 三个服务共 412 个现成的只读 Tool，认证和分页都处理好了，凭证只放在本机 .env | 给 AI 一个能写入的账号或接口 | AI 理解错了就可能改到数据，事后也说不清它做过什么 | 只读白名单写在代码里，没有任何写入能力，每次调用都进审计日志 | 直接读底层数据库表 | 要懂表结构和字段含义，读出来的是原始数据，容易漏掉业务规则 | 优先走 SAP 标准业务接口（BAPI、标准 OData 服务、Released API），结果带着业务含义；RFC 服务里的查表 Tool 只作只读补充 | 用大白话说，它的好处是 不用记事务码：直接问「这张 PO 为什么还没付款」，AI 会自己查订单、发票和供应商未清项。 只读，改不了数据：RFC 调用必须通过 98 个标准读取函数的白名单，HTTP 只发固定的 GET 请求（唯一的 POST 是获取 OAuth token），没有任何创建、修改或过账的能力。 密码不经过 AI：密码、client secret 和 token 只放在本机的 .env 里，在错误信息和日志中显示为 [REDACTED]；Tool 不接受凭证、任意 URL 或原始 OData 查询，TLS 校验始终开启。 查过什么都有记录：每次调用都会写进 logs/toolcallsYYYY-MM-DD.jsonl，包括参数、状态、耗时和用到的函数或 API 路径，用 gettoolcalllog 就能回看。 查不到就说查不到：每个结果都带 ok、notfound、partial 或 error 状态。空列表不等于余额为零，缺权限不等于没有数据，清账参考不等于实际付款。 三种部署都能接：本地部署和私有云走 RFC/BAPI 或 OData，公有云走 Released API；三个服务的配置、凭证和日志互相独立。 用你已经在用的 AI 工具：Claude Desktop、Claude Code、Cursor 等支持 MCP 的客户端都能直接连，不需要另外搭平台或写 Agent。 它不做什么 为了说清楚边界：SAP Data MCP 只读，不创建、不修改、不过账、不审批任何单据；它调用 SAP 标准接口，不会去操作 SAP GUI 或 Fiori 页面；它返回 SAP 给出的数据，不替你下结论，比如不会把清账参考当成付款记录。它也不是 SAP 官方产品，能查到哪些数据，取决于目标系统激活了哪些服务、登录用户有哪些权限。 包含什么 服务和客户端标签 | 适用系统 | 接入方式 | 只读 Tool | privatecloud/rfc sapprivaterfc | 开放 RFC 的 S/4HANA Private Edition、On-Premise；ECC / NetWeaver | RFC/BAPI，PyRFC + SAP NW RFC SDK | 95 个，基于 98 项 RFC 函数白名单 | privatecloud/odata sapprivateodata | 开放标准 OData 服务的 Private Edition、On-Premise | OData V2/V4 over HTTPS | 159 个（155 业务 + 4 基础） | publiccloud/api sappublicapi | S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition | Released OData V4/V2 API over HTTPS | 158 个（154 业务 + 4 基础） | 三个服务合计注册 412 个只读 Tool（不同服务之间有不少同名 Tool），覆盖 8 大标准模块：MM/IM、PP、SD、WM/EWM、FI、CO、主数据 / MDG、QM。RFC 服务另有 Basis 和接口监控（ST22、SM21、SLG1、SM37、IDoc、qRFC/tRFC/bgRFC 队列、Gateway 服务注册），以及只读查表、只读查看源码和运行已审核的只显示报表。各模块的详细覆盖、接口来源和已知缺口见 docs/COVERAGE.md（英文）。 可以这样问 「PO 4500000417 的货款怎么还没到？」：订单、订单历史、供应商发票、供应商未清项。 「今天系统里有哪些短转储？」：listshortdumps（RFC）。 「今天早上以来有没有被取消的后台作业？」：listbackgroundjobs（RFC）。 「列出最近三天出错的入站 IDoc。」：listidocs（RFC）。 「物料 4000123 在 1010 工厂各库存地点、各批次有多少库存？」：RFC 用 searchmaterialstock，HTTP 服务用 getmaterialstock。 「供应商 100318 在公司代码 1710 下有哪些未清项？」：searchsupplieraccountitems。 结果保留 SAP 原始的字段名、键、金额、单位和币种，零值和 false 也照样返回。列表用 maxresults 和 offset 分页。监控类时间是 SAP 应用服务器本地时间，与 SAP GUI 显示一致。 目录结构 文档 docs/COVERAGE.md：按模块列出的覆盖范围、接口选择及 SAP 官方出处、已知边界（英文）。 privatecloud/rfc/README.md：RFC Tool 及对应的 SAP 函数、所需权限、审计日志字段。 privatecloud/rfc/docs/GOLDENPATH.md：RFC 从安装 Python 到第一次调用的完整步骤。 privatecloud/odata/README.md 和 publiccloud/api/README.md：两个 HTTP 服务的服务映射。 测试 tests/ 里的离线回归测试使用 SAP 形态的样例数据，不登录 SAP。RFC 部分的测试会导入 PyRFC，请在装好 RFC 依赖的环境里运行： 新增 RFC 函数时，先确认它是标准只读函数，再加入 READONLYFUNCTIONS；不在名单上的函数会被 Connector 直接拒绝。 声明 独立开源项目，与 SAP SE 无隶属关系，也未获其认可。SAP、S/4HANA 及其他 SAP 产品名称是 SAP SE 的商标。宣传片中的业务数据为演示虚构。 License MIT
